Hierarchical Clustering

No centroids. No K upfront. Just repeated merging — from n individual customers down to one giant cluster, one pair at a time, with the full tree of every possible K built along the way.

01 · nutshell revision

Class 01 & 02, in three sentences

K-Means

Pick K starting points → assign every customer to its nearest centroid → move each centroid to the mean of its assigned customers → repeat until nothing changes.

K-Means++

Only changes where K-Means starts: farther-away points get picked with higher probability (weighted by distance²) as starting centroids, so runs become far more stable and repeatable.

The unresolved problem

Even with perfect initialization, K-Means still assumes one centroid can represent a whole cluster — so rings, crescents, and unequal-density groups still break it, no matter how good the starting point is.

Where we left off, word for word: "if centroids are the real limitation, what's a completely different way to group customers — one that doesn't rely on a single 'center' at all?" Today answers that question.
02 · the motivation

Why hierarchical clustering — a completely different idea

Instead of guessing K centers up front and assigning points to them, what if we just started joining the two most similar customers together, one pair at a time, and kept going until everyone belongs to one giant group?

No centroids. No K upfront. Just repeated merging. That single sentence is the entire idea of hierarchical clustering — everything else today is detail on top of it.

Why this is a genuinely different tool, not just "K-Means without K"

K-Means / K-Means++Hierarchical Clustering
Needs K upfront?Yes, alwaysNo — K is chosen after seeing the full structure
Uses a centroid?Yes, every cluster has oneNo — clusters are built purely from pairwise distances
OutputOne flat partition into K groupsA full hierarchy — every possible K from 1 to n, all at once
Can undo a bad merge?Reassigns freely every iterationNo — once two points are merged, that merge is permanent
03 · the two flavours

Two types of hierarchical clustering

Agglomerative (bottom-up)

Start with every point as its own cluster. Repeatedly merge the two closest clusters. End with everyone in one cluster. This is the one actually used in practice — and where today's class spends almost all its time.

Divisive (top-down)

Start with everyone in one cluster. Repeatedly split the "worst" cluster into two. End with every point as its own cluster. Conceptually the mirror image of agglomerative — covered in Section 6, mostly for completeness since it's rarely used in production as-is.

Both build the exact same kind of output — a tree of nested clusters, called a dendrogram — just constructed in opposite directions.
04 · agglomerative, mechanically

Agglomerative clustering — from n clusters to 1

Take n customers. At the very start, every single customer is their own cluster — n clusters for n points. At the very end, after enough merges, everyone belongs to one giant cluster. Everything in between is the interesting part.

6 customers we'll use for every worked example today — 2 natural groups {A,B,C} and {D,E,F}, deliberately simple enough to compute by hand.

The merge countdown

StepWhat happensClusters remaining
StartEvery point is its own clustern = 6
Merge 1Merge the 2 closest clusters (points, at this stage)n − 1 = 5
Merge 2Merge the next 2 closest clustersn − 2 = 4
.........
Merge n−1The last two remaining clusters merge1
Exactly n−1 merges, always — no more, no less, regardless of what the data looks like. Going from n individual points down to 1 giant cluster requires precisely n−1 merge operations, one merge at a time. This number (n−1) will matter again in Section 08 when we look at the linkage matrix's shape.

Seeing it happen — the actual points, merging based on distance

WHAT YOU SEE: the SAME 6 points at 4 different moments — start (6 clusters), after merge 1, after merge 2, and the very end (1 cluster). NOTICE: the dashed circle at each stage shows exactly which points have been grouped together so far, and the height label shows the actual distance that triggered that merge. WHY THIS MATTERS: "merge the two closest clusters" isn't abstract — B and C merge first because they're genuinely the closest pair (distance 0.860), not because of any ordering rule.

The 4-step loop, in plain English

1
Start: every customer is its own cluster.
2
Find the two closest clusters, merge them into one.
3
Repeat: find the next two closest clusters (which may now include the cluster you just created), merge again.
4
Keep going until every customer belongs to one giant cluster.
The one question this raises immediately: "closest clusters" is easy when both are single points — that's just a distance calculation. But once a cluster has 2 or more points inside it, what does "distance between two clusters" even mean? That question is the entire subject of Section 05.
05 · the central question

How do you merge? — Linkage methodologies

Once a cluster has more than one point in it, "distance between two clusters" needs a precise definition. Four different definitions are in standard use — each answers "how close are these two clusters?" in a genuinely different way, and each has situations where it shines and situations where it quietly breaks.

⚠ The one rule that never changes, no matter which linkage you use: once you have a distance number for every pair of clusters, you always merge the pair with the SMALLEST (minimum) distance. This is true for single, complete, average, and Ward alike — the four methods only disagree on how that distance number itself is computed. "Complete linkage" means the distance between two clusters is a maximum (of point-pairs inside them) — it does NOT mean you merge the pair with the biggest number. You still always merge whichever pair of clusters is closest right now.
LinkageDistance between two clusters =
Singledistance between their closest pair of points
Completedistance between their farthest pair of points
Averagethe average distance across all pairs of points
Wardthe increase in total within-cluster variance after merging

1 — Single Linkage (Nearest Neighbor)

$$D(A,B) = \min_{a \in A,\, b \in B} d(a,b)$$

Look at every point in cluster A against every point in cluster B, and take the single smallest distance found. Two clusters are "close" the moment even one pair of their members is close — regardless of how different the rest of the two clusters are.

Worked computation, our 6-point set: suppose {A,B,C} is one cluster and {D,E,F} is another. Here are all 9 cross-cluster pairwise distances:

PairDistancePairDistancePairDistance
A-D8.485B-D7.569C-D7.500
A-E8.387B-E7.500C-E7.529
A-F9.759B-F8.846C-F8.780
Single linkage takes the minimum of all 9 — that's 7.500 (tied between B-E and C-D, gold-highlighted above). So $D(\{A,B,C\},\{D,E,F\}) = 7.5$ under single linkage. Remember: this 7.5 then goes into the merge decision — whichever pair of clusters has the smallest such distance is what actually gets merged next.
Key idea: single linkage looks only at the minimum (closest) distance between points of two clusters. It can create long, chain-like clusters by linking nearest neighbours.
WHAT YOU SEE: two real, well-separated blobs connected by a thin trail of bridge points. NOTICE: single linkage's cluster sizes come out 103 vs. 2 — it chained straight through the bridge and swallowed almost everything into one cluster. WHY: single linkage only ever needs ONE close pair to justify a merge — the bridge provides an unbroken sequence of close pairs, so the "closest point" test never objects, all the way from one real blob to the other.

When it fails: exactly the scenario above — "chaining" through noise, bridges, or a few nearby outlier points, merging clusters that should stay separate.

When to use it: when true clusters are non-convex, elongated, or ring/crescent-shaped (Section 09 proves this directly) — and when you're confident the data has no thin bridges of noise connecting unrelated groups.

2 — Complete Linkage (Farthest Neighbor)

$$D(A,B) = \max_{a \in A,\, b \in B} d(a,b)$$

The mirror image of single linkage: look at every pair across the two clusters, and take the largest distance. Two clusters only count as "close" if even their most different pair of members is still reasonably close.

Worked computation, same 6 points: the same 9 cross-cluster distances from Single Linkage above:

PairDistancePairDistancePairDistance
A-D8.485B-D7.569C-D7.500
A-E8.387B-E7.500C-E7.529
A-F9.759B-F8.846C-F8.780
Complete linkage takes the maximum of all 9 — that's 9.759 (A-F, gold-highlighted). So $D(\{A,B,C\},\{D,E,F\}) = 9.759$ under complete linkage. Notice this is a much larger number than single linkage's 7.5 for the exact same two clusters — complete linkage is inherently more "pessimistic," which is precisely why it resists chaining. Remember: the "maximum" is only how this ONE number (9.759) was computed. When comparing this pair against other cluster pairs to decide what to merge next, you still merge whichever pair has the SMALLEST such number.
Key idea: complete linkage is conservative — it looks at the worst-case (maximum) distance between points, so it tends to create tighter, more compact clusters than single linkage.

When it fails: can be overly conservative — a single distant outlier inside an otherwise tight cluster inflates the "farthest pair" distance and can prevent two genuinely related clusters from merging, or force premature splitting of one real cluster.

When to use it: when you want tight, roughly-equal-sized, compact clusters and specifically want to avoid the chaining failure mode above.

3 — Average Linkage

$$D(A,B) = \dfrac{1}{|A||B|}\sum_{a \in A}\sum_{b \in B} d(a,b)$$

Take every cross-cluster pair, average all of those distances. Where $|A|$ and $|B|$ are the number of points in each cluster.

Worked computation, same 6 points: average the same 9 cross-pairs:

PairDistancePairDistancePairDistance
A-D8.485B-D7.569C-D7.500
A-E8.387B-E7.500C-E7.529
A-F9.759B-F8.846C-F8.780
Sum = 74.355Average = 74.355 ÷ 9 = 8.262
Notice 8.262 sits neatly between single linkage's 7.5 and complete linkage's 9.759 — exactly what "average of everything" should do. Remember: as always, this 8.262 is only useful once compared against the distances of OTHER cluster pairs — merge whichever pair is smallest.
Key idea: average linkage looks at the average of all cross-cluster distances. It balances single linkage (too sensitive to outliers) and complete linkage (too strict), often producing clusters of moderate size and shape.

When it fails: can still be pulled around by cluster size imbalance — averaging over a cluster with 200 points vs. one with 3 points can behave counter-intuitively since every one of those 600 cross-pairs counts equally.

When to use it: a solid, reasonable default when you're not sure single or complete is right — genuinely a middle-ground choice, not just a compromise for its own sake.

4 — Ward Linkage

Ward asks a completely different question from the other three: "if I merge these two clusters, how much would total within-cluster variance increase?" — then picks whichever merge causes the smallest increase.

$$\Delta(A,B) = \dfrac{|A||B|}{|A|+|B|} \lVert \mu_A - \mu_B \rVert^2$$

where $\mu_A, \mu_B$ are the centroids of the two clusters, and $\lVert\cdot\rVert^2$ is squared Euclidean distance — yes, this brings a centroid back in, but only as an internal bookkeeping device for the merge decision, not as something points get assigned to the way K-Means does.

Worked computation, same 6 points:

StepCalculationResult
Centroid of {A,B,C}((1+1.5+1)/3, (1+1.8+2.5)/3)(1.167, 1.767)
Centroid of {D,E,F}((7+7.5+8)/3, (7+6.3+7.8)/3)(7.5, 7.033)
Squared distance between centroids(7.5−1.167)² + (7.033−1.767)²40.11 + 27.73 = 67.84
Ward's Δ(3×3)/(3+3) × 67.84 = 1.5 × 67.84101.76
Remember: Ward's Δ (101.76) plays the exact same role as the other three linkages' numbers — compute it for every pair of clusters, then merge whichever pair gives the SMALLEST Δ (the smallest increase in variance).
Key idea: Ward prefers merges that keep clusters compact and similar in size. It minimizes the increase in total within-cluster variance at each step — often producing balanced, near-spherical clusters compared to single or complete linkage.

When it fails: exactly like K-Means, Ward implicitly assumes roughly spherical, similar-sized clusters — it inherits K-Means's shape limitation almost entirely (proven directly in Section 09).

When to use it: the standard default for well-behaved, roughly-blob-shaped business data (customer segmentation, RFM) — it's what produced the cleanest dendrogram in Section 04's toy example, and it's what we'll use for the RFM walkthrough in Section 11.

Side-by-side summary — when each one is actually the right call

LinkageBest forWatch out for
SingleNon-convex, elongated, ring/crescent shapesChaining through noise/bridges (Section 09's proof)
CompleteTight, roughly equal-sized compact clustersOne outlier can distort or block a correct merge
AverageGeneral-purpose default, moderate cluster shapesCan behave oddly with very unequal cluster sizes
WardBusiness/RFM-style data — balanced, spherical segmentsSame shape limitations as K-Means

So which linkage do I actually pick? (Simple answer, no theory required)

Short answer: no, don't always default to Ward blindly — but you also don't need to know the "true" shape in advance. You can't eyeball a 6-, 20-, or 50-feature dataset the way you eyeball a 2D scatter plot, so don't try. Instead, use the exact same trial-and-compare habit you already use for choosing K — just apply it to linkage too.
1
Start with Ward. It's the sensible default for typical business/customer data — most real segments (spending tiers, usage patterns) are roughly round, similarly-sized groups, which is exactly what Ward is built for. Fit it, cut the dendrogram, look at the cluster profiles.
2
Get suspicious of Ward if: the dendrogram forces very unbalanced groups together (e.g. one giant cluster + tiny slivers), or the resulting segment profiles don't make business sense, or you have a specific reason to suspect non-round structure (e.g. a fraud/anomaly pattern that "trails off" rather than clustering tightly).
3
When suspicious, just try Single and Average too — they're one line of code each (Section 05's formulas). Cut each at a comparable K.
4
Compare using Silhouette Score — exactly the same metric from Class 01/02. Whichever linkage gives the best Silhouette and cluster profiles that make sense to the business is the one you keep. If they all agree, great — that's confirmation. If they disagree, that disagreement itself is useful: it tells you shape genuinely matters for this dataset.
The one line to remember: Ward is a good starting guess, not a rule — try 2-3 linkages, let Silhouette Score and business sense pick the winner, exactly like you already do for choosing K.

The full worked dendrogram for our 6-point set

Ward linkage's actual merge sequence on the 6-point set: (B,C) merge first at height 0.860, then (D,E) at 0.860, then A joins (B,C) at 1.359, then F joins (D,E) at 1.585, and finally the two big groups merge at 14.267 — cutting at height 3 (dashed gold line) cleanly recovers the 2 true groups.
06 · the mirror image

Divisive clustering — top-down, splitting instead of merging

Agglomerative merges its way from n clusters down to 1, in exactly n−1 operations. Divisive is the exact mirror image: it starts with all n points as ONE single cluster, and repeatedly splits a cluster into two, continuing until every point is its own cluster — n clusters. Same tree, opposite direction, same n−1 count of operations (this time splits, not merges).

AgglomerativeDivisive
Starting pointn clusters (every point alone)1 cluster (all n points together)
Ending point1 cluster (all n points together)n clusters (every point alone)
OperationMerge the 2 closest clustersSplit the "worst" cluster into 2
Number of operationsn − 1 mergesn − 1 splits
In practice, you almost never run divisive clustering all the way to n clusters. Just like you don't need agglomerative's dendrogram to fully collapse to 1 cluster before you find a useful K, divisive clustering is normally stopped early, the moment it reaches whatever K you actually want. The full "1 → n" description above is the complete conceptual algorithm; the worked example and code below both stop early, at a chosen K, exactly as would happen in practice.

How does a "split" actually happen?

What "worst" means here — SSE, the same idea as WCSS under a different name. SSE stands for Sum of Squared Errors — for one cluster, it's the sum of squared distances from every point in that cluster to that cluster's own centroid. This is exactly Class 01's WCSS formula, just computed for a single cluster in isolation rather than summed across all clusters at once. "Highest SSE" simply means: of all the clusters that currently exist, which one is the most spread out / least cohesive right now? That's the one that gets split next.

The most common real implementation: bisecting K-Means. At every level, take whichever current cluster has the highest SSE (the most spread-out, least cohesive one), and run plain K-Means with K=2 on just that cluster's points — nothing more exotic than that. The two resulting sub-clusters replace the one you split. Repeat until you have as many clusters as you want.
1
Level 0 (the start): all n points are one single cluster. SSE of this one cluster = WCSS of the whole dataset.
2
Level 1: only one cluster exists, so it's automatically the "worst" one. Run K-Means (K=2) on the whole dataset → 2 clusters, each with its own SSE.
3
Level 2: compare the SSE of the 2 existing clusters, pick whichever is higher, run K-Means (K=2) on just that cluster's points → now 3 clusters total, and you compute a fresh SSE for each of the 2 new sub-clusters.
4
Repeat: at every level, compare SSE across all current clusters, always split whichever has the highest SSE right now, until you reach the desired K (or, if you never stop, all the way to n clusters, each with SSE = 0).
WHAT YOU SEE: level 0 (all data, 1 cluster — the true starting point) → level 1 (K-Means K=2 on everything) → level 2 (the highest-SSE cluster gets split again) → continuing until we stop at K=6 (not all the way to n — see the callout above on why real usage stops early). NOTICE: each split is a small, local, plain K-Means call — the "hierarchical" part is purely the bookkeeping of which cluster's SSE is highest and gets split next.

Code — optional, for completeness

# scikit-learn ships bisecting K-Means directly -- this IS divisive clustering from sklearn.cluster import BisectingKMeans model = BisectingKMeans(n_clusters=6, random_state=42) labels = model.fit_predict(X) # internally: repeatedly calls plain KMeans(n_clusters=2) on whichever # existing cluster has the highest SSE (Sum of Squared Errors -- the same # idea as WCSS, just for one cluster), replaces it with the 2 sub-clusters, # and repeats until n_clusters is reached (stopping early, per the callout above).
Why divisive is rarely used in production, honestly: at level 1, deciding how to split all n points into 2 is itself a full K-Means run on the entire dataset — expensive, and subject to K-Means's own initialization sensitivity at every single split. Agglomerative, by contrast, only ever needs pairwise distances computed once upfront. This is why almost everything from here on (dendrogram analysis, linkage, RFM) uses agglomerative — divisive is good to know conceptually, but agglomerative is what you'll actually reach for.
07 · reading the tree

Analyzing the dendrogram — how do you actually find K?

Hierarchical clustering's algorithm never outputs a single K on its own — it builds the entire tree, every possible K from 1 to n, all at once. Choosing K is a separate, deliberate step you do after the tree is built, by deciding where to "cut" it.

Direct answer to "does the algorithm give K by default": No. The raw output is the full merge sequence (the linkage matrix, Section 08) — a horizontal cut line at some height is what turns that tree into an actual K-way partition. You choose the height; scipy/sklearn just execute the cut.

How to actually choose where to cut

1
Plot the dendrogram. Every merge is a horizontal line at the height (distance) at which it happened.
2
Look for the tallest vertical gap between consecutive merges — a long vertical line with no merges crossing it means the next merge required a big jump in distance to happen, i.e. it joined two genuinely dissimilar groups.
3
Draw a horizontal cut through that gap. The number of vertical lines the cut crosses = your chosen K.

Stop here — do NOT confuse this with K-Means's WCSS elbow

These are two different curves, computed two completely different ways, that happen to look similar and get called "the elbow" by everyone. Mixing them up is one of the most common points of confusion in this whole topic, so let's separate them explicitly, side by side, before going any further.
WHAT YOU SEE: the SAME 20-point dataset, plotted two ways. LEFT (K-Means): at every K, K-Means is completely re-run from scratch with new random centroids, and WCSS is computed for that fresh fit. RIGHT (Hierarchical): the tree is built once; every point on this curve is just read off the same already-built dendrogram at a different cut height — no re-fitting happens at all. NOTICE: both curves bend and flatten in a broadly similar shape — that's why people conflate them — but the mechanism behind each point on the curve is entirely different.
K-Means's WCSS ElbowHierarchical's Merge-Height Elbow
What's plottedWCSS (Class 01's formula) at each KThe linkage distance at which each merge happened
How each point is obtainedRe-run K-Means from scratch, with new random initialization, for every single KRead directly off ONE already-built dendrogram — zero re-fitting
Sensitive to random seed?Yes — different seeds can shift the curve (Class 02's instability problem)No — the tree was built once, deterministically, from the linkage matrix
Cost to generate the whole curveK separate full K-Means fitsFree — it's just reading numbers already sitting in the linkage matrix
The one sentence to keep them straight: K-Means's elbow answers "how does re-fitting the model at each K change its tightness?" — hierarchical's elbow answers "how far apart were the two things that got merged, at the moment they merged?" Same-looking bend, completely different question underneath.

Is there a way to plot merge-height vs K directly? Yes.

Exactly analogous in spirit to K-Means's elbow curve, but computed the hierarchical way described above — take every merge height from the linkage matrix and plot it against the K that existed right before that merge happened.

WHAT YOU SEE: merge height on the y-axis, number of clusters remaining on the x-axis, computed from a real 20-point, 4-true-cluster dataset. NOTICE: there's a dramatic jump in height right around K=3→K=4 — that's the dendrogram's own "elbow," found exactly the same way K-Means's WCSS elbow is found in Class 01.

Is this guaranteed to find the best K?

No — and our own example above proves it. This dataset was generated with 4 true clusters, but the biggest jump in merge height actually points to K=3. The heuristic isn't wrong mathematically — it correctly found the biggest jump — but "biggest jump" and "true number of groups" aren't guaranteed to be the same thing. Two of the four true clusters here happened to sit close enough together that merging them didn't cost much height, so the "big jump" appeared one merge later than the true structure.

So what do you do when it's not guaranteed?

1
Cross-check with Silhouette Score — cut the dendrogram at several candidate K's (the top few biggest jumps, not just the single biggest) and compute Silhouette at each, exactly like Class 01's combined Elbow+Silhouette approach.
2
Look at multiple candidate cuts, not just one — the dendrogram shows you the 2nd-biggest and 3rd-biggest jumps too; inspect the resulting cluster profiles at each candidate K, not just the top-ranked one.
3
Bring in domain knowledge and business constraints — exactly as in Class 02: if the business can only act on 3 segments, that's a legitimate reason to prefer K=3 over a mathematically-suggested K=4, provided the merge is a sensible one.
The honest summary: the merge-height elbow is a strong, principled first guess — not a guarantee. Treat it exactly like K-Means's own elbow curve: a starting hypothesis to validate, not a final answer to accept blindly.
08 · what actually gets computed

The linkage matrix — how the dendrogram is actually generated

A dendrogram is just a picture. The real output of agglomerative clustering is a table of numbers called the linkage matrix — the dendrogram is drawn directly from it, row by row.

The format — 4 columns, one row per merge

ColumnMeaning
idx1ID of the first cluster being merged
idx2ID of the second cluster being merged
distancethe linkage distance between them (Section 05's formulas)
sample_counthow many original points now live inside the newly-formed cluster
The indexing trick that confuses people: for n points, indices 0 to n−1 refer to the original data points. Every new merged cluster gets the next available index — so the first merge (of two original points) creates cluster index n, the second merge creates index n+1, and so on. A row like [3, n, height, 5] means "point 3 merged with the cluster created at merge index 0."
WHAT YOU SEE: the exact ID-assignment chain for our 6-point set, spelled out one merge at a time. NOTICE: the original 6 points keep IDs 0-5 forever — they never change. Every merge afterward creates the very next integer (6, 7, 8, 9, 10) as the ID for the new cluster it just formed. WHY THIS MATTERS: once you see this counting rule explicitly, any row in any linkage matrix becomes readable at a glance — an index ≥ n always means "a cluster formed at merge number (index − n)," never an original point.

So where does the ACTUAL membership of a merged cluster live?

Direct answer: it's not stored anywhere in the matrix Z. The linkage matrix only ever stores 4 numbers per row — idx1, idx2, height, count. It never stores "cluster 8 = {A, B, C}" as an explicit list anywhere. This is the part that trips people up, so let's be precise about what's really happening.
1
Membership is implicit, not stored. Cluster 8's members are never written down as a list — they're only reconstructable by tracing back through the matrix: row for ID 8 says "merge of 0 (=A) and 6"; ID 6 says "merge of 1 (=B) and 2 (=C)". Follow that chain down to indices below n, and you've reconstructed {A, B, C} — but only by walking the tree, never by a direct lookup.
2
During the algorithm's run, distances to a new cluster are updated with a formula — not recomputed from raw points. When B+C merge into a new cluster, the algorithm needs the distance from this new cluster to every other remaining cluster. It does NOT go back to the original coordinates of B and C and recompute from scratch. Instead it uses an update formula (called the Lance-Williams recurrence) that combines the already-known distances — e.g. for average linkage, the new distance is just a size-weighted average of the two old distances. This working table of "current distances between current clusters" is what actually drives the algorithm — and it's discarded once clustering finishes. Only the four numbers per merge (the history) survive into Z.
3
To retrieve membership after the fact, you don't read it off Z directly — you ask scipy to walk the tree for you. This is exactly what fcluster (already shown) and dendrogram do internally: they recursively expand every cluster ID back down to its leaf points, and hand you the final answer (a label per original point) — you never have to do the tree-walk by hand.
# You almost never need to manually decode cluster membership -- # scipy does the tree-walk for you. But here's what it's doing internally: def get_members(cluster_id, Z, n): """Recursively expand a cluster ID back down to original point indices.""" if cluster_id < n: return [cluster_id] # base case: it's an original point row = Z[cluster_id - n] # look up which merge created this ID left, right = int(row[0]), int(row[1]) return get_members(left, Z, n) + get_members(right, Z, n) # get_members(8, Z, 6) -- walks: 8 -> (0, 6) -> 0 is a leaf (A), 6 -> (1, 2) -> B, C # returns [0, 1, 2] i.e. {A, B, C} -- reconstructed, not looked up
The one sentence to remember: the linkage matrix is a history of merges, not a membership table — cluster contents are always recovered by walking that history backward to the original points, either by scipy's built-in functions or, as shown above, by a short recursive function doing exactly what they do.

Worked on our 6-point toy set (Ward linkage)

Merge #idx1idx2Distance (height)Sample countPlain English
01 (B)2 (C)0.8602B and C merge first — new cluster index 6
13 (D)4 (E)0.8602D and E merge — new cluster index 7
20 (A)61.3593A joins cluster 6 (B,C) — new index 8
35 (F)71.5853F joins cluster 7 (D,E) — new index 9
48914.2676the two big groups merge — everyone is now 1 cluster
Exactly n−1 = 5 rows for 6 points — matching Section 04's countdown exactly.

Watch it happen — the matrix and the tree, growing together

WHAT YOU SEE: the exact 6-point linkage matrix from above, playing out one row at a time — each row lights up gold in the table at the EXACT moment its merge appears as a new gold "∩" bracket in the dendrogram. NOTICE: row 0 (B+C, height 0.860) draws the first small bracket; row 2 (A joining the B-C cluster, height 1.359) draws a taller bracket around all three; the final row (height 14.267) draws the tallest bracket, joining the two halves into one tree. WHY THIS MATTERS: this is the literal, mechanical link between Section 08's numbers and Section 05's picture — nothing in the dendrogram is drawn from a separate process; every bracket IS one row of the matrix, at that row's own height.

Now the real thing — a full linkage matrix on 20 points

from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import linkage, dendrogram from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs X20, _ = make_blobs(n_samples=20, centers=4, cluster_std=0.6, random_state=7) Z = linkage(X20, method='ward') # Z.shape == (19, 4) -- exactly n-1 rows
Reading this table (n=20, so indices 0-19 = original points, 20+ = merged clusters): whenever you see an index of 20 or higher, that's a cluster formed at merge row (index − 20) — never an original point. For example, merge 6's "22" refers to the cluster formed at merge row 2 (points 11+13).

The gold-highlighted, asterisked values are all merged clusters, not original points — e.g. row 6's idx2="22*" is the cluster created at merge row 2 (22 − 20 = 2). Rows with two plain numbers (like merge 0: 5, 12) are the only rows merging two original points directly. Exactly 19 = n−1 rows total, as promised.
Notice the height jumps from 2.349 (merge 15) to 16.675 (merge 16) — a 7× jump. That's Section 07's "biggest gap" appearing directly as raw numbers in the matrix, before it's ever drawn as a picture.

From matrix to picture — the mapping is completely mechanical

WHAT YOU SEE: left, the 20 raw points with their index labels (matching the matrix above). Right, the dendrogram scipy draws directly from that matrix — every row becomes one "∩" shape at exactly the row's height, connecting whichever two branches idx1 and idx2 point to. NOTICE: nothing in the picture is invented — every merge height, every branch position, traces back to one row in the table on the left.
# Turning the matrix into an actual K-way cluster assignment from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import fcluster labels = fcluster(Z, t=4, criterion='maxclust') # cut the tree to get exactly 4 clusters # OR cut by height directly: labels = fcluster(Z, t=10, criterion='distance') # cut wherever height > 10
09 · the payoff

Where hierarchical clustering actually beats K-Means++

Class 02 proved K-Means++ still fails on moons and circles — better initialization never changes what shape a centroid can represent. Here's the direct, real-code comparison.

WHAT YOU SEE: K-Means++ and hierarchical clustering, run on the same Moons and Circles data. NOTICE: Ward-linkage hierarchical fails exactly like K-Means++ (same shape assumption, inherited directly from Section 05) — but single-linkage hierarchical cleanly separates both the crescents and the rings. WHY: single linkage never needs a centroid at all — it only asks "is there a chain of close neighbouring points connecting these two regions?" A ring or crescent is exactly a chain of close neighbours curving through space, which single linkage naturally follows and K-Means's centroid math cannot.
The precise, honest claim to make: "hierarchical clustering" isn't automatically better than K-Means on odd shapes — single linkage specifically is, because of how it defines cluster distance. Ward linkage inherits K-Means's exact same spherical-cluster assumption (Section 05's table already flagged this). The linkage choice, not the word "hierarchical," is what fixes the shape problem.
10 · a fair, direct comparison

Do outliers affect Hierarchical Clustering the same way as K-Means?

Short answer: yes, both are affected — but hierarchical clustering gives you a way to actually SEE it happening and fix it, which K-Means doesn't.

WHAT YOU SEE: two real customer segments plus one extreme outlier. NOTICE: at K=2, both K-Means and Ward-linkage hierarchical make the SAME mistake — the outlier merges with one real segment, corrupting it (Class 02's "outlier steals a centroid" failure, reproduced identically here). BUT: at K=3, hierarchical clustering cleanly isolates the outlier as its own singleton cluster (size 1), leaving both real segments (40 and 40 points) completely intact.

Why hierarchical clustering handles this better in practice

K-MeansHierarchical Clustering
Does the outlier distort a real cluster?Yes, at whatever K you pick — the mean gets draggedYes, at the SAME K — Ward still uses centroid-variance internally
Can you see it happening?No — you only get the final K labels, no visibility into whyYes — the dendrogram shows the outlier joining very LATE, at a very tall, isolated merge height
Can you fix it without re-running everything?No — must remove the outlier and re-fit K-Means from scratchYes — just cut the SAME dendrogram at a slightly higher K, the outlier peels off on its own, no re-computation needed
The practical workflow this enables: cut the dendrogram at K+1 or K+2 instead of your target K, check for any singleton or near-singleton clusters, treat those as candidate outliers (remove or investigate them), then cut again at your real target K. This diagnostic step is something K-Means structurally cannot offer, because it never keeps the full merge history — only hierarchical clustering's tree gives you this "undo history" to inspect.
11 · applying it to real data

Hierarchical clustering on ClusterMart's RFM data

The exact same Recency/Frequency/Monetary features from Class 02 — same business problem, same scaled data — run through Ward-linkage agglomerative clustering instead of K-Means.

from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import linkage, dendrogram, fcluster # RFM_norm is the SAME scaled (Frequency, Amount, Recency) table from Class 02 Z_rfm = linkage(RFM_norm, method='ward') dendrogram(Z_rfm, no_labels=True)
WHAT YOU SEE: the dendrogram for a sample of RFM-scaled ClusterMart customers. NOTICE: a clean, tall gap appears right around 4 clusters — cutting there (gold dashed line) recovers the same Premium / Frequent / Discount-Hunter / Occasional structure Class 02 found via K-Means and Elbow+Silhouette, this time discovered from a completely different mechanism with zero centroids involved.
# Turn the cut into actual customer segment labels segment_labels = fcluster(Z_rfm, t=4, criterion='maxclust') RFM['Segment'] = segment_labels RFM.groupby('Segment')[['Recency','Frequency','Amount']].mean()
What this cross-check buys you: two structurally different algorithms (centroid-based vs. merge-based) landing on the same 4-segment structure is much stronger evidence than either one alone — this is a genuine, practical version of the "stability check" from Class 02's validation pyramid, using a different algorithm instead of a different random seed.
12 · the honest tradeoffs

Limitations — when NOT to use hierarchical clustering

The core problem: it doesn't scale

Computing every pairwise distance between n points costs $O(n^2)$ memory and the full clustering costs $O(n^2 \log n)$ to $O(n^3)$ time, depending on the linkage method. For n=20,000 customers, that's 400 million distances just to start — for n=1,000,000, it's a trillion. K-Means, by contrast, costs roughly $O(n \cdot K)$ per iteration — linear in n, which is precisely why it scales to millions of rows and hierarchical clustering typically cannot.
Data sizeHierarchical clusteringK-Means / K-Means++
Up to ~10,000 rowsComfortable on a laptopComfortable
10,000 – 100,000 rowsSlow, memory-heavy; needs a capable machineStill fast
100,000+ rowsUsually impractical directlyScales fine, or use MiniBatchKMeans

Other limitations worth knowing

LimitationWhy it happens
Merges are permanentOnce two points are merged, there's no "undo" — a bad early merge (Section 05's chaining failure) can propagate through the rest of the tree
Choice of linkage matters a lotSection 05 showed 4 genuinely different distance definitions — picking the wrong one for your data's true shape gives a wrong answer confidently
No probabilistic/soft membershipEvery point belongs to exactly one cluster at each cut, just like K-Means — no "70% Premium, 30% Frequent" style answer (that's what GMM is for)

What to do at large-scale production instead

1
Use hierarchical clustering for exploration on a sample, never as the production algorithm on full-scale data (elaborated fully in Section 13).
2
For production-scale clustering itself, use K-Means/K-Means++ (or MiniBatchKMeans for very large data, from Class 02).
3
If you specifically need hierarchical clustering's tree structure at scale, look at scalable variants like BIRCH (Balanced Iterative Reducing and Clustering using Hierarchies), which builds a compact summary tree in one pass and can approximate hierarchical clustering on much larger data — worth knowing exists, not covered in depth today.
13 · the practical question every team asks

"My data is large and the shape isn't spherical — do I just give up and use K-Means anyway?"

This is exactly the tension Section 09 and Section 12 create: hierarchical clustering handles odd shapes better, but can't run on large data at all. Does that mean large, non-spherical data is simply stuck with K-Means's worse-fitting results?

No — and defaulting to K-Means here without a fight gives up real accuracy for no good reason. There's a well-established middle path used in production exactly for this situation.

The workflow: sample → hierarchical → K → K-Means on full data

1
Take a representative sample of the large dataset — small enough for hierarchical clustering to run comfortably (e.g. 5,000–10,000 rows out of a 2-million-row dataset).
2
Run hierarchical clustering on the sample, using whichever linkage method fits the suspected true shape (Section 05/09) — this is cheap, since the sample is small.
3
Read K off the sample's dendrogram (Section 07's merge-height elbow, cross-checked with Silhouette).
4
Run K-Means (or K-Means++) on the FULL dataset, using that sample-derived K as the fixed cluster count.
Is this a legitimate approach? Yes — this is standard practice, not an improvised workaround. It's a genuine, well-founded experimentation strategy: hierarchical clustering's job here is purely K discovery on a scale where it's cheap and reliable, while K-Means's job is purely fast, scalable assignment using a K that's already been validated. You get hierarchical clustering's structural insight and K-Means's scalability, without paying either one's full cost.

What this workflow does NOT fix

Be precise about what you actually gained. You've solved the "what's the right K" problem using a better exploratory tool. You have not solved K-Means's shape assumption on the full dataset — if the sample's dendrogram told you the true shape is crescent-like (best captured by single linkage), running plain K-Means on the full data with the "right" K will still draw round decision boundaries through those crescents (Section 09's exact failure). The workflow fixes the K-selection problem, not the shape-representation problem — if shape is the core issue, the honest fix is a scalable shape-aware algorithm (DBSCAN, or approximate methods like BIRCH — Balanced Iterative Reducing and Clustering using Hierarchies), not K-Means with a better K.
What you're trying to fixDoes sample→HC→K→KMeans help?
"I don't know what K to use on my large dataset"Yes — exactly what this workflow is for
"My clusters are crescent/ring-shaped and K-Means draws straight lines through them"No — K-Means still can't represent that shape, no matter how good K is
14 · everything in one page

Class 03: the complete picture

1

No centroids, no K upfront

Start with every point as its own cluster, merge the closest pair, repeat n−1 times until one cluster remains.

2

Linkage defines "closest"

Single (min), Complete (max), Average (mean), Ward (variance increase) — four genuinely different answers to the same question.

3

The dendrogram IS the algorithm's output

A linkage matrix with exactly n−1 rows — K is chosen afterward, by cutting, not handed to you upfront.

4

Single linkage beats K-Means on shape

No centroid needed — it follows chains of near neighbours, exactly what rings and crescents are made of.

5

Outliers affect both — HC shows you the damage

The dendrogram lets you literally see an outlier isolate as a late, tall, singleton merge — K-Means gives no such visibility.

6

It doesn't scale — that's the real tradeoff

$O(n^2)$ or worse vs. K-Means's near-linear cost — the entire reason the sample→HC→K→KMeans workflow exists.

K-Means++Hierarchical
SpeedFast, scales to large dataDoesn't scale as well
Need K upfront?YesNo — decide from the dendrogram
Cluster shapeSpherical/convex onlyHandles more complex structures (with the right linkage)
Best forLarge, frequently-refreshed datasetsSmaller, exploratory analysis — and K-discovery for later K-Means runs

The one-sentence mental model

K-Means asks "which center is each point closest to?" Hierarchical clustering never asks that question at all — it only ever asks "which two things, right now, are most alike?", one pair at a time, all the way up.
